newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - VW wows German stock market with 97 outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - VW wows German stock market with 97 outlook.

text.p: Europe's largest carmaker Volkswagen was the darling of the German stock exchange on Friday as its shares soared to record highs on an extremely upbeat outlook for 1997 and a series of analysts' upgrades.
VW shares hit an all-time high of 1,117.50 marks, a rise of over twelve percent, in bourse trade in Frankfurt and analysts said the share could head as high as 1,500 marks this year.

It slipped from the highs later in the day as profit-taking kicked in, but still ended with marked gains. VW closed the bourse session at 1.072.50 marks, up 76.50 marks or 7.68 percent, before easing to 1,049 marks in post-bourse dealings.

The share's dramatic rise began on Thursday, when Volkswagen kicked off 1997 by forecasting better first quarter earnings due to a 9.5 percent rise in sales and said it expected higher profits and turnover for the year.
Shares penetrated the 1,000 mark level for the first time shortly after the results were announced. They continued to strengthen after analysts met Volkswagen and emerged bullish.
A rash of earnings upgrades followed, as well as hikes in share price targets for the year, and Volkswagen advanced strongly early on Friday.
Guenter Dielmann, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Research, said DMG had raised its 1996 EPS to 55 marks from 33 marks, to 65 marks from 43 marks for 1997 and to 86 marks from 65 marks for 1998.
"The recommendation for the stock remains overweight," Dielmann told Reuters. There was room for "clearly positive development" in the share price, he said.
Other analysts also saw further upside scope for the share, despite the bout of profit-taking later on in the session.
Car analysts at ABN Amro in Frankfurt set a share price target for 1997 of 1,500 marks and said they were keeping their recommendation of strong buy for the share.
Francois Colli at Paribas in London said VW still looked cheap after the profit upgrade.

"The relative price/earnings ratio of 61 percent to 55 percent for 1997/98 is undemanding in view of the quality of the company. In addition, VW still offers a 40 percent discount to the European sector average on the basis of 1998 ratios. We recommend buying the stock," said Colli.
The company's 1996 results also got a hefty lift from the German mark's decline in currency markets.

Berenberg Bank in Hamburg said in a statement that the firmness of the dollar did much to bring the German car sector to the forefront of the stock market and recommends VW to long-term investors, alongside its previous favourite, Daimler-Benz AG.

Sabine Bluemel at IMI Sigeco in London said: "Trading on a 1998 multiple of 9.5 times, we believe Volkswagen shares are the most undervalued in the European automotive sector, trading on a 44 percent discount to the European sector average.
She set a share price target of 1,300 marks and maintained a buy recommendation.

VW said in its 1996 annual report that it expected "positive results" for 1997 despite forecasts for slow consumer spending as many European nations slash spending to qualify for European currency union set to begin in 1999.
Its 1996 results were hurt by a 1.5 billion mark ($870 million) charge to reduce the interest rate growth forecast for its pension funds to five percent from six percent.
If VW had not opted for the pension fund change, VW officials said the results would have been sharply above the doubling in 1996 group profit of 678 million marks.
